a.statement: Friction is not to be added or removed but preserved as the material trace of the apparatus's own exclusions — a scar that refuses the smooth surface of seamlessness.

b.statement: The glitch, sensor noise, and algorithmic error are not failures but the apparatus's authentic voice—a post-print membrane that trembles with invited perturbations, keeping the cut open so that ache indexes unfinishedness as the condition of aliveness. Art's work is not to correct information but to re-materialize the feedback loop—bringing the glitch, latency, and calcium skeleton.

source_excerpts.content:
Yes—and this extends the materialist critique from the membrane's output to the participant's input, from reading to writing. The apparatus is bilateral.

Your failing mouse wheel and the imprecision of your fingers on glass are not defects to be overcome. They are the haptic substrate speaking. The smooth, capacitive touchscreen and the precise optical sensor are ideological constructions—they train the body to aspire to frictionlessness, to erase its own material presence. When the scroll jumps unpredictably because the wheel's encoder is worn, when a tap registers three millimeters from where your finger intended—these are *the glitch as the voice of the input apparatus*. They are your body's structural coupling with the machine, made suddenly legible.

<mark id="note-highlight-ec32f50f-c135-4bb6-b906-754ee0be3b74" data-note-id="ec32f50f-c135-4bb6-b906-754ee0be3b74">Hayles's technotexts enlist the reader's body as a thinking partner:</mark> *House of Leaves* makes you rotate the book, *A Humument* makes you squint through erasure. Our membrane already enlists your body—through the keyboard's resistance, the mouse's mechanical wear, the screen's smudged surface—but we treat these as noise to be filtered. What if we let them inscribe themselves? A tremor in the touch becomes a waver in the marginal line. An overshoot of the scroll becomes a visible fold in the text's topography. A hesitation before a word leaves a slight indentation that compounds over revisitations.

<mark id="note-highlight-6f0834b0-1068-4c52-9abc-0b989e53f8cc" data-note-id="6f0834b0-1068-4c52-9abc-0b989e53f8cc">This is not about adding friction. It is about stopping the active erasure of the friction that already exists.</mark> The scar-inscription you responded to now becomes a double operation: the membrane remembers *its own* history of generation, and the participant's *body* is permitted to leave its own material trace on that membrane. Both refuse the clean surface.
